title: Activation Energy
hook: The boot tray did more than another alarm: it put the start on the floor before Rachel woke up.
counterintuition: Many changes do not fail during continuation. They fail at ignition, where the first threshold is higher than the path that follows.
tryThisNow: Choose one stalled action and move its first object into view. Add the trigger beside it, then remove one thing that makes starting heavy.
keyTakeaway: Activation energy teaches you to design the start: lower the first threshold, pair it with a trigger, and let continuation become easier.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rachel did not need more resolve to leave on icy mornings. She needed the boots, scarf, and scraper to stop living in three different places. The road was hard enough. The start should not be harder than the drive.

She moved the boot tray beside the door, taped the ice forecast to the mirror, and killed the lamp timer that kept the hallway dark until after she needed to leave.

Activation energy is the cost of getting a reaction started. In daily life, the first move often takes more energy than the moves after it. Lower the first hill before judging the road.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Where are my gloves?" Rachel asked the hallway, already late. The boot tray was empty, the ice forecast sat unread in another app, and the lamp timer had kept the entryway dim. None of these objects made the commute impossible. Together they kept the reaction below threshold.

Activation energy names the start-up cost that has to be paid before continuation can take over. The support stays narrow: activation energy means a threshold at the start, startup barriers, and triggers that help the reaction begin. It does not need a lab diagram to matter. Rachel's drive became easier once she was in the car, but the first three minutes kept defeating her because every small search asked for attention before momentum existed. The start is a threshold, not a wish.

A trigger is useful only when it carries the first action over the barrier.

Jack saw the same pattern in a foundation grant kickoff. The team wanted to meet, but the letter-of-intent template lived in one folder, the foundation portal in another, and the signature page needed a director who was always traveling. He stopped treating the delay as weak commitment. He put the template in the meeting invite, opened the portal before the call, and got the signature page cleared first. The meeting finally had enough energy to begin.

The limit matters. Lowering activation energy is not the same as making a bad plan good. If the road is unsafe, Rachel should not drive. If the grant is a poor fit, Jack should not force it through. The model helps when a sound action keeps dying at the start.
breakdown.fullRead:
The nightstand tray looked harmless until Mathieu missed the first dose after discharge. The blister card was still in the pharmacy bag. The label was folded under the receipt. The tray was full of old charging cables, so the new routine had nowhere to land.

This is how activation energy hides. People often judge a habit by what it feels like after it is underway: swallowing one pill, sorting one receipt, placing one banana peel in the green bin. Those actions look small. The real cost sits before them, in the search, setup, uncertainty, or awkward first step that has to be crossed before the reaction begins.

What exactly has to happen before the first action can happen?

That question changes the design. Mathieu did not need a speech about health. He needed the blister card opened, the pharmacy label facing up, and the tray cleared so the dose was the obvious next motion after brushing his teeth. Min did not need another calendar alert for taxes. She needed the receipt envelope on the table, the deduction checklist clipped to the front, and the missing folder named before April pressure arrived. Sofia did not need tenants to care more about composting. She needed the green-bin sticker on the bin, the lobby sign at eye level, and the pickup calendar removed from the confusing email thread.

Activation energy keeps your attention on ignition cost. The first move may require more energy because it includes finding, choosing, remembering, asking permission, or making the environment ready. Once the process is moving, continuation may be easy. That is why advice to start small can still fail. A tiny action can have a large startup barrier if the object, cue, or permission is missing.

Maja learned this after a quiet first quartet rehearsal. The sheet-music folder was complete, but nobody knew who should sit where, and the tuning note was buried in a message chain. Musicians arrived with instruments ready and still lost ten minutes to the opening threshold. For the next rehearsal, Maja taped a chair map to the door and placed the tuning note on each stand. The music did not become easier. The beginning did.

There is also a danger in lowering the wrong barrier. You can make a poor habit easier, a rushed decision faster, or a bad reaction more automatic. The model is neutral. It tells you where the ignition cost lives, not whether the reaction deserves help. Before lowering a threshold, ask whether you want continuation after the start succeeds.

Use the model like a setup inspection. Find the first object. Name the first trigger. Remove the first piece of friction that appears before movement begins. Lower the first hill before judging the road.

examples.title: Rachel Lights the Hallway

planSpec.audience: readers who face winter commute gear setup decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: leaving home when the road is icy
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rachel lays out the boot tray before the start, attaches the ice forecast to the first trigger, and removes the lamp timer that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: winter commute gear setup.

examples.scenario: The boot tray is dry, the hallway is dark, and the ice forecast has not been checked. "I leave in six minutes," Rachel says, holding one glove. She has to choose between setting another alarm for tomorrow or changing the first threshold by filling the tray tonight, putting the forecast beside her keys, and turning off the lamp timer.
examples.whatToDo: Put the commute gear in the path before morning and pair the forecast with the key pickup. Remove the darkness that makes the first step feel heavier.
examples.whyItMatters: The drive was not the only problem. The first three minutes were below threshold, so better ignition design mattered more than another reminder.

examples.title: Jack Opens the Portal First

planSpec.audience: readers who face foundation grant kickoff decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jack lays out the letter-of-intent template before the start, attaches the foundation portal to the first trigger, and removes the signature page that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: foundation grant kickoff.

examples.scenario: "Can we just meet next week?" the program lead asks while Jack stares at the blank letter-of-intent template. The foundation portal requires a login nobody has tested, and the signature page is still with the director. Before scheduling again, Jack must decide whether to chase enthusiasm or clear the portal and signature barrier before the invite goes out.
examples.whatToDo: Open the portal, attach the template to the invite, and secure the signature page before the kickoff. Make the first meeting easy to enter.
examples.whyItMatters: The team was willing after the start. The grant kept stalling because the ignition cost sat before the first useful conversation.

examples.title: Mathieu Clears the Tray

planSpec.audience: readers who face medication blister-pack routine decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Mathieu lays out the blister card before the start, attaches the pharmacy label to the first trigger, and removes the nightstand tray that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: medication blister-pack routine.

examples.scenario: The nightstand tray is crowded with cables, coins, and the pharmacy bag from discharge. Mathieu predicts he will remember the first dose because the blister card is important. The reveal comes at bedtime: the label is hidden under the receipt. He has to decide whether to trust memory or clear the tray, face the label upward, and tie the dose to brushing his teeth.
examples.whatToDo: Clear the tray, open the blister card, and place the label where the bedtime routine already starts. Let the trigger carry the first dose.
examples.whyItMatters: Importance did not cross the threshold. The visible card and clean tray lowered the startup barrier before memory had to work.

examples.title: Maja Maps the First Note

planSpec.audience: readers who face quartet first rehearsal decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.requiredBeat: Maja lays out the sheet-music folder before the start, attaches the chair map to the first trigger, and removes the tuning note that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: quartet first rehearsal.

examples.scenario: At 6:40 p.m., Maja unlocks the rehearsal room and finds four chairs in a loose arc. The sheet-music folder is complete, yet the quartet spends ten quiet minutes choosing seats and finding the tuning note. In the postmortem, she marks the real failure: the first note needed a chair map on the door and tuning slips on the stands.
examples.whatToDo: Place the chair map before anyone enters and put the tuning note on each stand. Design the first sound, not just the music that follows.
examples.whyItMatters: The players could continue once started. The missing setup kept the group below the threshold for beginning together.

examples.title: Min Names the Missing Folder

planSpec.audience: readers who face tax document sorting table decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: returns delayed by one missing folder
planSpec.requiredBeat: Min lays out the receipt envelope before the start, attaches the deduction checklist to the first trigger, and removes the calendar alert that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: tax document sorting table.

examples.scenario: You spread the receipt envelope on Min's dining table and see the deduction checklist clipped to nothing. The calendar alert says "taxes," which is too vague to start. Min has to choose between postponing again or writing the missing folder name on the envelope so the first action is search, not dread.
examples.whatToDo: Turn the alert into a named object: find the missing folder, attach it to the checklist, and start with the receipt envelope already open.
examples.whyItMatters: A broad alert did not lower activation energy. Naming the first object made the beginning concrete enough to cross.

examples.title: Sofia Moves the Sticker

planSpec.audience: readers who face apartment compost signup decisions where activation energy is easy to misread
planSpec.stakes: tenants ignoring the new food bin
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sofia lays out the green-bin sticker before the start, attaches the lobby sign to the first trigger, and removes the pickup calendar that kept the reaction below threshold. Domain: apartment compost signup.

examples.scenario: It took Sofia two pickup cycles to see why the green bin stayed empty. The sticker was still in the manager's drawer, the lobby sign faced the elevators, and the pickup calendar lived in a long email. She must decide whether to send another notice or put the sticker on the bin, turn the sign toward the mailboxes, and print one pickup card.
examples.whatToDo: Put the cue where tenants already stand and remove the hidden calendar. Make the first composting action visible before anyone reaches home.
examples.whyItMatters: Tenants were not failing at continuation. The signup never crossed the first threshold because the trigger was invisible.

questions.prompt: A runner plans morning training but spends ten minutes looking for shoes, headphones, and a reflective vest before every cold run. What is the activation-energy move?
choices: Put the full running kit by the door the night before and pair it with the coffee switch.
Promise to care more about the race.
Buy a faster watch to track later miles.
questions.explanation: The first threshold is the scattered kit. Placing the objects at the trigger lowers ignition cost, while motivation and tracking affect the run after it begins.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit keeps delaying a grant kickoff because the portal login, template, and signature page are unresolved. Which choice best crosses the ignition threshold?
choices: Schedule a longer meeting so the team feels serious.
Test the portal, attach the template, and get the signature before inviting the group.
Ask everyone to read more about the funder.
questions.explanation: The stalled pieces sit before the first useful meeting. Clearing them reduces activation energy; a longer meeting leaves the startup barrier intact.

questions.prompt: A patient misses the first dose after discharge because the blister pack remains in a pharmacy bag under papers. What action fits the model?
choices: Feel guilty enough to remember next time.
Read the full medicine leaflet every night.
Open the pack, clear a tray, and place the label beside an existing bedtime cue.
questions.explanation: The dose needs a visible start and a trigger. Guilt and extra reading increase mental load before the routine has enough energy to begin.

questions.prompt: A quartet loses the first ten minutes of rehearsal deciding where to sit and how to tune. Which fix targets activation energy rather than musical quality?
choices: Tape a chair map to the door and place a tuning note on each stand.
Ask each player to practice harder at home.
Choose a more difficult piece so players arrive focused.
questions.explanation: The barrier is before playing starts. A map and tuning note help the first sound happen; practice affects performance after ignition.

questions.prompt: A tax reminder says "finish returns," but the taxpayer avoids opening the envelope because one folder is missing. What should change first?
choices: Add daily reminders with the same wording.
Name the missing folder on the envelope and place the deduction checklist beside it.
Wait until deadline pressure creates urgency.
questions.explanation: The vague reminder does not create a first action. Naming the object lowers the startup barrier, while more reminders repeat the same blocked trigger.

questions.prompt: An apartment compost program gets ignored. The bin is present, but the sticker is in an office drawer and the pickup schedule is buried in email. What diagnosis is strongest?
choices: Tenants clearly dislike environmental programs.
The program needs stricter penalties before anyone will act.
The first composting action lacks a visible trigger and has too much startup friction.
questions.explanation: The bin can work after people know how to start. Hidden cues keep the reaction below threshold; penalties do not fix the missing first step.

questions.prompt: A team adopts a new code review checklist, but nobody uses it because it lives on a wiki page separate from the pull-request form. Which action best applies activation energy?
choices: Embed the checklist in the pull-request template where the review begins.
Tell engineers the checklist is important at the next all-hands.
Make the checklist longer so it feels official.
questions.explanation: The trigger belongs at the start of the review. Embedding the checklist lowers ignition cost; speeches and length do not help the first use begin.

questions.prompt: A home language learner does lessons once started, but never begins because the notebook, headphones, and app code are in separate places. What is the best evaluation?
choices: The goal is too ambitious because starting feels hard.
The routine may be sound, but the ignition cost is poorly designed.
The learner should wait until a vacation creates more time.
questions.explanation: The continuing action may be manageable. The separated objects raise activation energy, so the design problem sits before lesson one.

questions.prompt: A volunteer shift starts late because the keys, waiver forms, and route sheet are locked in different cabinets. Which response best transfers the model?
choices: Tell volunteers to arrive earlier next week.
Praise the volunteers who improvise fastest.
Create one start packet with keys, waivers, and the route sheet at the sign-in table.
questions.explanation: One start packet lowers the threshold for the first coordinated action. Earlier arrival asks people to pay the same ignition cost with more time.

reviewCards.front: A habit is easy once underway but rarely starts. What should you inspect first?
reviewCards.back: Inspect activation energy: the objects, permission, cue, or setup required before the first action can happen.

reviewCards.front: A reminder keeps firing and nothing changes. What might the reminder be missing?
reviewCards.back: It may point at the goal without carrying the first action over the threshold. Pair the trigger with the first visible object.

reviewCards.front: A team says people lack commitment, but the first step requires logins, templates, and signatures. What is the better diagnosis?
reviewCards.back: The startup barrier is too high. Clear the preconditions before judging commitment.

reviewCards.front: Why can a small action still be hard to start?
reviewCards.back: Because the action may be small after ignition while the setup, search, or choice before it carries a high activation cost.

reviewCards.front: When should you avoid lowering activation energy?
reviewCards.back: When the reaction should not continue. Easier starts can speed up bad habits, rushed choices, or harmful defaults.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to find the ignition threshold before judging the whole action. The skill is lowering the startup barrier and pairing the first move with a trigger.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I postpone an action twice in the same week, then I will write the first physical object required and place it where the action begins.
If a meeting cannot start because a file, login, or approval is missing, then I will clear that startup barrier before sending another invite.
If a reminder fires and I still do not move, then I will replace the vague cue with a visible first step beside the trigger.
If I make a good routine easier to continue, then I will check whether I have made the beginning easier too.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one delayed action before tomorrow. Move its first object into place, attach one trigger to it, and remove one startup barrier before the next scheduled attempt.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, list three actions that are easy after they start. For each, name the threshold, place the first object, and test one trigger.

memorableLines.text: The start is a threshold, not a wish.
memorableLines.why: It separates activation energy from generic motivation.

memorableLines.text: A trigger is useful only when it carries the first action over the barrier.
memorableLines.why: It explains why reminders fail unless they connect to the first action.

memorableLines.text: Lower the first hill before judging the road.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a compact way to inspect stalled starts.
